questions.question: What does it mean for $E$ to be sequentially compact in a metric space?
options: Every sequence in $E$ is constant, taking one value forever.
Every sequence has a subsequence converging in $E$.

questions.question: For sequential compactness, where must the subsequential limit lie?
options: Only in $\mathbb{R}$, regardless of the metric space
At the first term of the original sequence

questions.question: Which set is sequentially compact?
What can be concluded about any finite set in any metric space?
options: It is sequentially compact only in $\mathbb{R}^n$

questions.question: What equivalent notion is sequential compactness connected to in any metric space?
Which phrase best explains the interpretation of sequential compactness?
options: The set contains no convergent sequences.
The set has no infinite sequences
Closed under limits of subsequences of its sequences.
The set must be open and unbounded

questions.question: If every sequence in $E$ has a subsequence converging to a point of $E$, what can be concluded about $E$ in a metric space?
In a metric space, if $E$ is compact, what follows?
Why is the phrase 'to a point in $E$' essential for sequential compactness?
options: Limits are not allowed in metric spaces
A subsequence converging outside $E$ does not qualify.
Every sequence must converge to its first term.
The original sequence must be finite

questions.question: What warning is attached to the closed unit ball example?
options: It is never sequentially compact in $\mathbb{R}^n$
It is sequentially compact only when it is open
Its sequential compactness can fail in infinite dimensions

questions.question: A sequence in $E$ has a subsequence converging to $x$, but $x\notin E$. Does this alone prove that $E$ is sequentially compact?
options: No, the limit must lie in $E$
Yes, any convergent subsequence is enough
Yes, provided the original sequence is infinite

questions.question: Let $E$ be a noncompact subset of a metric space. Since compactness and sequential compactness are equivalent in metric spaces, what follows about sequential compactness of $E$?
What must every sequence in a sequentially compact set have?
options: A subsequence converging outside the set
A subsequence converging to a point in the set

questions.question: What is the limit requirement in sequential compactness?
options: The subsequence limit must lie outside the set itself.
The subsequence limit must belong to the same set.

questions.question: Which viewpoint is equivalent to compactness in metric spaces?
If $E$ is sequentially compact and $(x_i)$ is a sequence in $E$, what can be selected?
options: A subsequence $(x_{i_j})$ converging to some $x\in E$
A subsequence that converges to some point outside $E$
A finite subcover of the sequence
An open set containing no terms

questions.question: Which set is sequentially compact in $\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: An unbounded open ray such as $(0,\infty)$

questions.question: Why is a finite set sequentially compact in a metric space?
options: Every sequence in it is strictly increasing.
Any sequence has a constant subsequence at some point.
No sequence can be formed from it.
Every point in it is outside the set.

questions.question: What does sequential compactness say about limits of selected subsequences?
options: Every sequence must converge without passing to a subsequence.
It contains the limit of a convergent subsequence from every sequence.
Only sequences with distinct terms are considered.

questions.question: A sequence in a metric-space subset has no convergent subsequence with limit in that subset. What follows?
options: The subset is not sequentially compact.
The ambient metric space is not defined.
